description: Reconciliation of a single module is set arithmetic over immutable, content-addressed identifiers: M = (B u X u Y) \ ((B \ X) u (B \ Y)). Everything either side added is kept, and everything either side removed stays removed. A textual conflict is not representable, because modifying a block yields a different identity. The refusals matter as much as the results: a reconciliation proceeds only when the best common ancestor is unique.

vectors.name: both_sides_added
vectors.why: The ordinary case: a merge of two contributions keeps both. Nothing was removed, so the subtrahend is empty and the result is the union.

vectors.name: one_side_dropped_what_the_other_retained
vectors.why: Exclusion has precedence, and that is the point of the equation rather than a side effect. A block one side deliberately dropped must not return because the other side still held it -- otherwise every reconciliation would silently undo a removal.

vectors.name: both_sides_dropped_the_same_block
vectors.why: Agreement on a removal is still a removal. Stated because the equation reaches it by two different subtractions and both must land on the same answer.

vectors.name: re_adding_is_not_smuggling_it_back
vectors.why: Content addressing means re-registering the same source yields the same identifier, so the reconciliation recognizes it as something this brain removed rather than as a new contribution. Deliberately re-admitting it remains possible, and remains an explicit commit.

vectors.name: symmetric_in_the_two_sides
vectors.why: The mirror of the drop-vs-retain case. For a fixed ancestor the merge is symmetric, so which brain performs the reconciliation does not change its result.

vectors.name: empty_ancestor_is_a_union
vectors.why: With nothing in the ancestor nothing can have been removed, so the result is the union however the two sides differ.

refusals.name: no_common_ancestor
refusals.why: Two histories that share no ancestor have no three-way merge defined: a block present in one and absent from the other is ambiguous between 'they added it' and 'I dropped it', and those demand opposite outcomes. A conforming implementation MUST refuse with a distinguishable failure.

refusals.name: criss_cross_two_best_common_ancestors
refusals.why: A criss-cross history yields more than one best common ancestor -- common ancestors that are not themselves ancestors of another common ancestor. Equation 4 gives different results for different ancestors, so an implementation that silently picked one would be choosing the outcome. It MUST refuse with a distinguishable failure of its own, separate from having no ancestor at all.

topology.description: A and B are both best common ancestors of X and Y: neither is an ancestor of the other, and each is reachable from both heads.
